0.title: When the Soul Is Cast Down
0.essay:
If you are reading this from inside the dark, you are welcome here. This study is written slowly and gently, for those who feel low and cannot lift it, and for the friends, families and pastors who love them and want to help.

Not alone, and not forgotten

Depression is common, and it is common among Christians. It is not proof that you have no faith, or that God has given up on you. Some of the most faithful people in Scripture sank so low that they asked to die. God did not cast them off. He fed them, listened to them and kept them. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).

If you are in danger

If you are having thoughts of ending your life, please pause here and tell someone now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), or go to your nearest emergency department. Tell someone you trust, and see a doctor. Asking for help is not weakness or unbelief. It is the next right step, and your life is precious to God.

How to read this study

You do not have to read it all at once. If concentration is hard, read one section, or one verse, and stop there. The study Biblical Counseling has chapters for those giving care in depression and in suicidal crisis, and the studies Christian Suffering and Doubt & Faith say more about lament and about seasons when God feels silent. This study stays close to the depressed person, and to those who walk beside them.

The chapters

What Depression Is, and Is Not; Saints in the Dark; The Bruised Reed; Small Steps in the Valley; Friends Who Stay; and Hope That Holds When Feelings Do Not.

For reflection

Are you reading this for yourself, or for someone you love? What would you most like God to show you through it?

1.title: What Depression Is, and Is Not
1.essay:
Depression is more than a bad day or a sad week. It is a heavy, lasting lowness that drains the colour out of life, and it touches the whole person: body, mind, circumstances and walk with God. Understanding it is the first kindness we can show.

What it can feel like

Doctors use the word depression for symptoms that last for weeks rather than days: a low mood that will not lift; losing pleasure in things once enjoyed; sleeping too little or too much; tiredness that rest does not fix; poor concentration; feelings of worthlessness or heavy guilt; hopelessness; and sometimes thoughts of death. It ranges from mild to severe. Many people say it feels less like sadness than like numbness, or a fog, or a weight on the chest.

Scripture knows this. “My tears have been my food day and night” (Psalm 42:3). “I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel” (Psalm 31:12).

The whole person

God made us body and soul together. He “formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). So depression rarely has one tidy cause. Several strands usually twist together.

The body plays its part: illness, hormonal change (including after childbirth), thyroid problems, chronic pain, some medicines, family history and the workings of the brain. The mind plays its part: habits of thought that are harsh, all or nothing, always expecting the worst. Circumstances play their part: bereavement, losing work, loneliness, conflict, abuse, or years of caring for someone else. And the spiritual life is involved: guilt, doubt, fear of God’s anger, and sometimes sin. Often the darkness causes the spiritual struggle rather than the other way round. A person who cannot concentrate finds prayer hard, and may wrongly decide that God has left.

Not simply sin, not simply weak faith

Some Christians assume that depression always means unconfessed sin or a lack of faith. Scripture will not let us say that. When the disciples asked whose sin had caused a man’s blindness, Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents” (John 9:3). Job’s friends were sure his suffering proved hidden sin, and God said they were wrong.

Sin can play a part. David wrote, “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3), and he found relief when he confessed. But much depression is suffering, not sin. To treat a sufferer as a rebel is to lay a heavier load on someone already crushed.

Doctors and medicine

If you have been low for more than a couple of weeks, see a doctor. That is no failure of faith. Luke was “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), and Paul told Timothy to take a little wine “for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments” (1 Timothy 5:23). We pray for our daily bread and then eat it; we can pray for healing and take the tablets.

Antidepressants help many people, especially when depression is moderate or severe. They do not change a person’s standing with God or replace trust in him. Often they lift the fog enough for someone to sleep, think and pray. Talking therapies help too. Medicine is not a cure-all, and it should never be stopped suddenly without a doctor’s advice. A Christian need neither idolise it nor despise it.

A disputed question

Some Christians hold that depression is at root a spiritual problem, sin or unbelief, so that medicine only masks it. Others treat it as a purely medical disorder, about which the church has little to say beyond prayer and kindness. Each sees something real: the first that every human need reaches down to our relationship with God, the second that the body is truly involved.

This commentary’s view: Scripture is sufficient for the care of souls, and our deepest need is always spiritual: to know God through Jesus Christ. That is as true of the cheerful as of the depressed. Yet the body matters, so depression calls for a medical check alongside wise pastoral care; psychiatric care and medication have their proper place; and much depression is suffering rather than sin. The pastor and the doctor are allies, not rivals.

If you are thinking about ending your life

Depression can make death seem like the only way out. It is not, and that thought is a symptom of the illness, not the truth about you. If you have such thoughts, tell someone today: a friend, a family member, a pastor or a doctor. If you feel you might act on them, call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America), ring a crisis line such as Samaritans (116 123) or 988 in the United States, or go to an emergency department now. You are not a burden to the people who love you.

An example

A deacon in his fifties lost his job. Within months he was waking at four every morning, could not pray and dreaded church. Sure it was a spiritual failure, he told no one, until his wife persuaded him to see the doctor, who found an underactive thyroid as well as depression. With treatment, regular visits from his pastor and the patience of two friends, the fog slowly thinned. The hardest step, he said later, was admitting he was ill.

For reflection

Which strands of depression (body, mind, circumstances, spiritual life) do you most easily overlook? Why do you think Christians sometimes feel ashamed to see a doctor? How does John 9:3 guard us from quick judgments about suffering? Who would you tell if you began to think about ending your life?

2.title: Saints in the Dark
2.essay:
The Bible does not hide its saints’ darkest hours. Prophets, poets and apostles tell us plainly that they wanted to die, that they could not sleep, that God seemed far away. God kept their words in his book so that we would never think we are the first, or that darkness means we are lost.

Elijah: “I, even I only, am left”

After the victory on Mount Carmel, Elijah ran for his life from Jezebel. He sat under a broom tree and prayed, “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers” (1 Kings 19:4). The study Biblical Counseling shows how God first gave him sleep and food. Look now at what happened next.

At Horeb God asked a gentle question: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (1 Kings 19:9). Elijah’s answer shows how depression bends the way we see things: “I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life” (1 Kings 19:10). He said it twice. It felt true, but it was not. God had kept “seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal” (1 Kings 19:18). The LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in “the sound of a low whisper” (1 Kings 19:12). He did not shout at his tired servant. Then he gave him work to do and a companion, Elisha, to walk with him. God corrected Elijah’s lonely conclusion with the truth, with a purpose and with a friend.

The psalmist: thirsty and far from home

Psalms 42 and 43 belong together, joined by a refrain that comes three times. The writer once led the crowds to worship (Psalm 42:4). Now he is far away, mocked by people asking, “Where is your God?” (Psalm 42:3). He feels drowned: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Psalm 42:7). Yet in the same breath he says, “By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me” (Psalm 42:8), and he prays, “Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me” (Psalm 43:3). He is low and he is holding on, both at once.

Psalm 88 goes further down and does not come back up. It ends, “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). That a psalm like this is in Scripture is itself a mercy: the study Christian Suffering explores it more fully. Even a prayer with no happy ending is still a prayer addressed to “God of my salvation” (Psalm 88:1).

Job and Jeremiah: cursing the day

Job, a righteous man, lost his children, his wealth and his health. He cried, “Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?” (Job 3:11). He could not rest: “the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn” (Job 7:4). Anyone who has lain awake with a heavy heart knows that line.

Jeremiah was faithful through years of rejection. He felt the word of God like “a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9), and he asked, “Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed?” (Jeremiah 15:18). In one chapter he sings, “Sing to the LORD; praise the LORD!” (Jeremiah 20:13), and a verse later he cries, “Cursed be the day on which I was born!” (Jeremiah 20:14). Real faith can swing that fast, and Scripture records both.

Paul: despairing of life

Even the apostle Paul wrote, “we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself” (2 Corinthians 1:8). He did not hide it from the church. And he saw a purpose in it: “that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9). The God who raises the dead can raise a person from despair.

In the history of the church

Charles Spurgeon, the Baptist preacher of Victorian London, suffered deep depression for much of his ministry, made worse by illness and by grief after a disaster at one of his services in 1856, when panic in a crowded hall left several people dead. He spoke openly about it, and gave a lecture to his students on the fainting fits that can come upon ministers. The poet William Cowper, who wrote “God moves in a mysterious way” and “There is a fountain filled with blood”, suffered terrible depression all his life. He came to faith while being cared for in an asylum, and his friend John Newton stood by him for many years. These were not weak Christians. They were sufferers whom God used.

What their stories teach

Faithful people can fall very low. God did not reject any of them for it. He listened, corrected gently, sent help and kept them. A young woman who had been depressed for months found Psalm 88 for the first time. She read it twice and wept, not from despair but relief. “I didn’t know you were allowed to pray like that,” she told her pastor. It became the door through which she began to pray again.

For reflection

Which of these believers is most like you, or like someone you love? How did God answer Elijah’s “I only am left”, and what lonely conclusions might you need to test against the truth? Why do you think God kept Psalm 88 in the Bible? How does Paul’s honesty in 2 Corinthians 1:8–9 help the church today?

3.title: The Bruised Reed
3.essay:
“A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench” (Isaiah 42:3). Of all the pictures of Christ in the Bible, few are kinder to the depressed. This is how the Lord deals with people who can barely stand.

A bent reed and a smoking wick

A reed by the river is a fragile thing. Once it is bruised and bent it is useless, and most people would snap it off and throw it away. A lamp wick that has burned low gives more smoke than light, and most people would pinch it out. Isaiah says the Servant of the LORD will do neither. He will not finish off what is already broken. He will not put out what is barely alight.

Matthew tells us who this Servant is. When the Pharisees were plotting against Jesus, he “withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all” (Matthew 12:15). Then Matthew quotes Isaiah: “a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory” (Matthew 12:20). This is not a theory about Jesus. It is a description of how he treated real people, crowds of the sick and weary, and how he treats you.

The Puritan Richard Sibbes wrote a little book on this verse, The Bruised Reed, in 1630. His point was simple and deeply comforting: Christ does not despise small and weak beginnings of grace. Where there is even a little smoke, there is some fire, and he will tend it, not quench it.

Christ in Gethsemane

On the night before he died, Jesus took three friends into the garden, and “he began to be sorrowful and troubled. Then he said to them, ‘My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me’” (Matthew 26:37–38). Luke adds that an angel came, “strengthening him”, and that “being in agony he prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22:43–44).

We must be careful here. Jesus was not ill, and his sorrow was not sin or unbelief. It was the holy anguish of the sinless Son about to drink the cup of God’s judgment for us. But it means that the Lord knows from the inside what a crushing weight of sorrow is. He knows what it is to feel near death with grief. He knows what it is to ask friends to stay close, and to find them asleep. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). In the days of his flesh he “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7). Your tears are not foreign to him.

Isaiah called him “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3). Think of it: the eternal Son, through whom the stars were made, chose to become a man who wept. On the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). He went into the deepest darkness of all, bearing our sin, so that no one who trusts him will ever be truly forsaken.

He remembers that we are dust

God does not expect from a bruised reed what he expects from an oak in full leaf. “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:13–14). He knows that you cannot do today what you once did easily. He is not standing over you with a list.

And the dark does not hide you from him. “Even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day” (Psalm 139:12). You may not see him. He sees you clearly, and he has not looked away.

His grip, not yours

Depression often whispers that you have lost your faith, or that you are holding on so weakly that you will surely let go. But the Christian is not kept by the strength of his grip on Christ. He is kept by Christ’s grip on him. “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). The smouldering wick does not keep itself alight. The Servant tends it, and Isaiah adds that he “will faithfully bring forth justice” (Isaiah 42:3). He finishes what he starts. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

When you cannot pray

An elderly widow, deeply depressed after a long illness, told her pastor that she could no longer pray. “All I can say is, ‘Lord, have mercy.’” He read her the promise that “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Then he said, “That short prayer is a real prayer, and it is one the Lord loves to answer. And when you have no words at all, the Spirit is praying for you.” She said it was the first time in months that she had felt God might not be disappointed in her.

For reflection

In what ways do you feel like a bruised reed or a smoking wick? What does Matthew 12:15–20 show about how Jesus treats weak people? How does Christ’s sorrow in Gethsemane change the way you think about your own sorrow? Why is it a comfort that you are kept by Christ’s grip rather than your own?

4.title: Small Steps in the Valley
4.essay:
When Elijah collapsed, God’s first gifts were sleep, bread and water. Grace often comes through very ordinary means. Recovery from depression is usually not one great leap but many small steps, taken slowly, with help.

Care for the body

Because we are body and soul together, caring for the body is not unspiritual. It is part of honouring the God who made us.

Sleep. Try to go to bed and get up at about the same times each day, even when you do not feel like it. Keep screens out of the last hour before sleep. “He gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2): rest is a gift to be received, not a reward to be earned. If sleep is badly broken, tell your doctor.

Food and drink. Depression often steals the desire to eat, or drives a person to comfort-eat. Simple, regular meals help. Alcohol lowers mood further, and it can make dark thoughts more dangerous, so it is wise to avoid it.

Daylight and movement. A short walk outside each day, even ten minutes, can do quiet good. Regular exercise is known to help many people with mild and moderate depression. Start very small.

Rest. Jesus said to his tired disciples, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while” (Mark 6:31). If you are depleted by overwork, rest is obedience, not laziness.

Routine and small steps

Depression shrinks the day. Everything feels too much, so nothing gets done, and then guilt makes it worse. A simple routine helps: get up, wash, dress, eat breakfast, do one small task, go outside, contact one person. Write them down and tick them off. These are not little things. On a dark day, getting dressed is a real act of faithfulness, and the Lord who “knows our frame” (Psalm 103:14) sees it.

Try not to make large decisions while you are very low, such as leaving a job, a church or a marriage. Depression distorts judgment, as it distorted Elijah’s. Wait, and take counsel.

Honest prayer and lament

“Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). You do not need tidy or cheerful prayers. Tell God exactly how it is. When you have no words, borrow the psalmist’s: “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). Short prayers are real prayers. Read a few verses rather than a chapter, or listen to the Bible read aloud. The aim is not to perform but to keep turning your face towards God, however dimly.

Answering the dark thoughts

Elijah was sure he was alone. He was wrong. Depression produces thoughts that feel certain but are false: “I am useless.” “Everyone would be better off without me.” “God has finished with me.” It can help to write such thoughts down, and then, perhaps with a friend, set beside each one what God says. “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). You may not feel the truth yet. Say it anyway, as the psalmist spoke to his own soul.

Do not walk alone

Depression pulls us into hiding. Fight that pull gently. Keep going to church, even if you sit at the back and slip out early. Come to the Lord’s Table, where Christ feeds weak believers. Tell one or two trusted people the truth. “Woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!” (Ecclesiastes 4:10).

Seek counsel. A wise pastor or trained biblical counsellor can help you look at your thoughts, your circumstances and your walk with God. Keep seeing your doctor, and take medicine if it is prescribed. A Christian counsellor or therapist who respects your faith can also help. These are not rival paths. Use the help God provides.

A plan for the worst days

If you have ever had thoughts of ending your life, make a simple safety plan with someone you trust while you are calmer. Write down the warning signs, the people you will call, and the crisis numbers: emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America), Samaritans on 116 123, or 988 in the United States. Ask someone to help remove or lock away anything you might use to harm yourself. If the thoughts become strong, do not wait: call, tell, go. Reaching for help is exactly what God wants you to do.

An example

A university student stopped going to lectures and spent whole days in bed. Her church small group leader helped her book a doctor’s appointment and went with her. Together they made a list for each day: shower, breakfast, a walk to the corner shop, one psalm, one text to a friend. Some days she managed only the first two. Her leader told her that was enough. Over the term the list grew, and so did her strength.

For reflection

Which part of caring for your body is hardest for you at the moment? What small step could you take today? What dark thought keeps returning to you, and what does God say about it? Who could you ask to help you make a plan for the worst days?

5.title: Friends Who Stay
5.essay:
When Job’s three friends heard of his troubles, they came and “sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great” (Job 2:13). It was the best thing they did. Things went wrong when they started talking.

The gift of presence

Most depressed people do not need a clever answer. They need someone who will come, sit with them, and come back. Presence says what words often cannot: you are not alone, you are not too much, I am not leaving. “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Christ himself did this: at the grave of his friend, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35), though he was about to raise him.

Paul, worn out and “afflicted at every turn”, says that God, “who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus” (2 Corinthians 7:5–6). Notice how God comforted his apostle: by sending a friend. Often you are the means by which God answers someone’s prayer for comfort.

Job’s friends: a warning

Job’s friends were sincere and religious, and they said many true things about God. But they were sure they knew why Job was suffering. He must have sinned, they argued, and if he would only repent all would be well. Job called them “miserable comforters” (Job 16:2). At the end, God said to Eliphaz, “you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7). The man who complained honestly was nearer the truth than the men who explained confidently.

The warning is plain. Do not diagnose someone’s soul from the outside. Do not assume hidden sin. Do not hurry them out of their grief so that you can feel better.

No quick fixes

“Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day” (Proverbs 25:20). Cheerful words at the wrong time do not warm; they chill. Avoid sentences like “Just pray more”, “Cheer up, it could be worse”, “You have so much to be thankful for” or “Real Christians don’t get depressed.” Even true things, said too quickly, can sound like a door closing.

Better words are often simple: “I’m so sorry.” “I don’t understand it all, but I’m here.” “Would it help if I came round on Thursday?” “I’m praying for you, and you don’t need to reply.” Later, when trust has grown, there will be time for gentle truth from Scripture, one verse at a time.

Practical love

Depression makes ordinary tasks feel huge, so practical help is real love. Bring a meal. Offer a lift to the doctor and sit in the waiting room. Take the children for an afternoon. Invite them for a walk. Send a short message that asks nothing back. Keep inviting, even when they say no. Love that keeps showing up speaks of a God who keeps showing up.

Patience for the long haul

Paul’s instruction is wise: “encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). Depression can last months, and it can return. Friends grow tired, and the sufferer feels it. Pace yourself, share the care with others, and pray for staying power. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). The law of Christ is the law of the One who bore our heaviest burden all the way to the cross.

When you are worried about suicide

If you fear a friend may be thinking of ending their life, ask them plainly: “Are you thinking about killing yourself?” Asking does not put the idea in their head, and it often brings relief. If the answer is yes, take it seriously. Do not promise to keep it secret. If they are in immediate danger, stay with them and call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America), or take them to an emergency department. Otherwise help them contact their doctor or a crisis line today, such as Samaritans (116 123) or 988 in the United States, and stay in close touch. The study Biblical Counseling gives fuller guidance for pastors.

What churches can do

Churches can make it easier to be honest. Preach the laments as well as the praises. Pray publicly for those who are struggling in mind. Speak of depression without shame, and say plainly that seeing a doctor is wise. Let pastors and elders visit and keep visiting, and know the local services they can point to. And care for the carers: husbands, wives and parents of the depressed are often exhausted and alone.

A man in one church sent his depressed friend the same short text each morning for nearly a year: a verse, and “Thinking of you. No need to reply.” His friend rarely answered. Years later he told the man that on several mornings that text was the only reason he got out of bed.

For reflection

When you are with someone who is suffering, are you more tempted to explain or to stay? What did Job’s friends get right in Job 2:13, and what did they get wrong later? Which practical kindness could you offer someone this week? How could your church make it easier for people to admit they are struggling?

6.title: Hope That Holds When Feelings Do Not
6.essay:
“My soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is” (Lamentations 3:17). The writer of Lamentations had watched Jerusalem fall. Yet a few lines later he says, “But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope” (Lamentations 3:21). Christian hope does not wait for feelings to return. It rests on God.

Hope is not a feeling

Depression can drain away every feeling of hope, and some believers conclude that they have lost their faith. But hope in Scripture is not first a mood. It is confidence in a Person and in his promises. “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23). Those words were true when the writer felt them, and true when he did not.

Isaiah speaks to exactly this case: “Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God” (Isaiah 50:10). Notice that this person fears God and obeys him, and still walks in darkness. Darkness is not proof that God is displeased. The call is not to manufacture light, but to lean on God in the dark.

“I shall again praise him”

Three times in Psalms 42 and 43 the writer asks his soul why it is cast down, and three times he answers, “Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God” (Psalm 43:5). He does not yet feel the praise. He looks forward to it. Hope reaches into the future and borrows its light. “Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning” (Psalm 30:5). The night may be long, but it is not the last word.

An anchor out of sight

Hebrews calls our hope “a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain” (Hebrews 6:19). An anchor does its work out of sight, under the water. The ship may be tossed about, and the sailors may not be able to see what holds them, but the anchor holds. Our anchor is fastened where Jesus has gone before us, in the very presence of God. It does not depend on how the waves feel today.

So Paul could say, “I am sure that neither death nor life … nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). Depth is on that list. No depth of darkness is deep enough to separate a believer from God’s love in his Son.

Honest about this life

Many people do recover from depression, often more fully than they dared to believe. It is right to hope and pray for that. But Christians must be honest: some carry it for years, and it can return. William Cowper wrote hymns that have strengthened millions, yet in his last years he was convinced that God had cast him off, and he died in great darkness in 1800. Those who loved him trusted that the Lord who had saved him did not let him go, whatever Cowper felt. Our salvation rests on Christ’s finished work and his keeping power, not on the state of our minds on our final day. He is “able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (Jude 24).

The morning that is coming

Paul, who had despaired of life, wrote, “So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). He called his sufferings “light” and “momentary” only because he set them beside “an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17). One day God himself “will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore” (Revelation 21:4). Depression will not follow anyone into that city. The glory of God will be its light and the Lamb its lamp, and the long night will be over for good. What a Saviour, who took our darkness on himself so that we might have that morning!

Until then, Micah’s words can be ours: “when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me” (Micah 7:8).

If hope feels gone

If you feel that there is no hope at all, and thoughts of death are pressing in, please hear this: hopelessness is a symptom of the illness, not a verdict on your life. Tell someone today. Call your doctor, a crisis line such as Samaritans (116 123) or 988 in the United States, or the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America). Let others hold hope for you until you can hold it again.

An example

A mother of three went through two long seasons of depression in ten years. In the worst months she could not feel God at all. She kept a card by her bed with Lamentations 3:22–23 on it, and on many nights she read it without believing it. Looking back, she says, “I didn’t hold on to God. He held on to me. The card was just to remind me.”

For reflection

What is the difference between feeling hopeful and having hope? How does the picture of an anchor in Hebrews 6:19 help you in dark seasons? Why is it a comfort that our salvation does not depend on the state of our minds? Which promise in this chapter could you write on a card and keep close?
